title: The conquerors
hook: emperors who conquered every land, with drums beating, also went without the Name (Savaiye)

segments.voice: Yesterday, maate matang, and your line, they left empty-handed. Did the barefoot king lighten any wanting? And here's a small milestone: three hundred sixty-five days on this path. A whole year of days. Day three hundred sixty-five.

Before you see an army in the old world, you hear it. A low thudding comes over the hills, then another and another, until the ground itself seems to be beating. Kettledrums, war drums, the big nagaras, carried in front of the march so every village knows who's coming. The sound alone could make a city open its gates. Kings had them beaten when they set out and beaten again when they came home with a new country in their pocket. Now listen for the moment after the march has passed, when the last drumbeat rolls away down the valley. Today: the conquerors.
screen: `A THUDDING OVER THE HILLS.` → `NAGARAS IN FRONT OF THE MARCH.` → `THE LAST BEAT ROLLS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Among the ten savaiye is a verse made of that sound. In paraphrase: they went out and conquered every land in every direction, with drums and kettledrums beating. Their elephants trumpeted, their horses neighed by the thousand. Kings like these, past, present and to come, can't even be counted. And then the turn, the same turn the savaiye keep making: without remembering the Lord, at the end they all went to their final home. Another savaiya stands right beside it, about warriors in shining armor, so sure of themselves they thought even mountains couldn't move them. They too go. Here's the striking thing about the man writing it. Guru Gobind Singh had a great drum of his own. Sikh tradition remembers the Ranjit Nagara, a huge kettledrum made at Anandpur, beaten morning and evening, and its boom worried the hill kings around him. Sikhs still beat a nagara at some gurdwaras and in processions today. So this isn't someone who hated drums. He knew exactly how they sounded, and how good it felt to hear your own. What the verse is saying is simpler and harder. The sound of victory is real, and it fades. The conquerors are measured not by how far their drums carried, but by whether they remembered the One who outlasts every march. In the Sikh view, that remembering, simran, is the only thing that keeps sounding after the last beat. It's why the verse is said in the quiet of early morning, before the day's own drums start up: the deadlines, the targets, the scoreboards. They're allowed to beat. The verse just counts how long each one lasts.
screen: `THEY CONQUERED EVERY LAND.` · `WITHOUT THE NAME, THEY STILL WENT.` · `THE GURU'S OWN GREAT DRUM.` · `VICTORY IS REAL, AND IT FADES.` · then, large: `DRUMS FADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one small ambition. Sit and breathe slowly, and listen for a minute to whatever sounds are around you, near and far. Notice how each one rises and fades. Now find one small thing you've been pushing for that's mostly about being seen to win. More likes. The last word in an argument. Being first. Hold it lightly, like a drumbeat that's already rolling away. You don't have to give up every goal. Just set this one down, for today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you let it go. The bell holds the time.
The conquerors. A savaiya of kettledrums and conquered lands: kings beyond counting, who at the end still went without the Name.
Your line: drums fade. Today, when you hear a sound fade, a car passing, a song ending, a door closing, let it remind you which of your drums you can stop beating. Day three hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this among the Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning, and the nagara, the great kettledrum, is still beaten at some gurdwaras and in Sikh processions.

pairs: the remembering that outlasts the march

myth: Guru Gobind Singh wrote this verse because he disliked drums and armies
tradition remembers his own great drum, the Ranjit Nagara. he knew the sound of victory, and that it fades.
the verse says the conquerors are beyond counting
kings past, present and to come can't be counted, and without the Name they all still went.
the savaiya says ambition itself is forbidden
it measures the conquerors by whether they remembered the Lord, not by whether they marched.

fork.setup: you're a king. your drums have carried your name across every land and your horses number in the thousands. what does the savaiya say comes next?
options: without the Name, at the end you go, like the rest.
fork.reveal: the verse lets the drums beat and the elephants trumpet, then follows the kings to their final home. without remembering the Lord, the march ends where every march ends.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nagaare, kettledrums, among the drums beating in this savaiya's conquering march.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse against war.
what it means: the drums of victory are real and they fade; the conquerors are measured by whether they remembered the Lord.
what a scholar hears: the writer kept a great drum of his own, the Ranjit Nagara, so the verse speaks from inside the world of courts and campaigns, not from outside it.

sources.ref: Akal Ustat, Tav Prasad Savaiye (the savaiya of conquest with drums, and the savaiya of armored warriors)

sources.work: Sikh historical tradition (e.g., Kesar Singh Chhibber, Bansavalinama; Bhai Santokh Singh, Suraj Granth)

notes: The drum savaiya (jeet phire sabh des disaan ko baajat dhol mridang nagaare ...) paraphrased; usually counted as one of savaiyas 3–7. The voice says 'among the ten' without a number. Confirm its place and the paraphrase of its last line.
The armored-warriors savaiya (sudh sipaah durant dubaah ...) mentioned briefly as standing beside it. Confirm.
Ranjit Nagara: tradition dates it to the 1680s at Anandpur and says its sound alarmed the hill rajas (Bhim Chand of Bilaspur). Given as 'Sikh tradition remembers'. Confirm.
Nagara still beaten at some gurdwaras and in processions (nagar kirtan): confirm.
